sections.normalized_html:
We factor in two steps:

  1. Separate the greatest common factor from each of the terms. In this case, [MATH: \textrm{GCF}(6a,30) = 6,] so: [MATH: 6a + 30|=; (6 ⋅ a) + (6 ⋅ 5)]

  2. Place the common factor in front of the parentheses, leaving whatever remains inside the parentheses: [MATH: (6 ⋅ a) + (6 ⋅ 5)|=; 6(a + 5)]

Thus, the factored form of the expression is [MATH: 6(a+5).]

Thus, the factored form of the expression is [MATH: -5(a+7).]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Factoring is the opposite of distributing. To illustrate, consider the expression [MATH: 4(a-2b).] If you consider distributing as going forward,
[MATH: 4(a − 2b)|=; 4 ⋅ a − 4 ⋅ 2b|=; 4a − 8b,]
then factoring would be going in reverse:
[MATH: 4a − 8b|=; (4 ⋅ a)−(4 ⋅ 2b)|=; 4(a − 2b)]

Content:
In this case, you would say that [MATH: \color{red}4] was factored out of [MATH: 4a-8b.]

Content:
To factor any expression, we just need to follow these two steps:

Content:
1. Separate the greatest common factor from each of the terms (ignoring any negative signs). In this case, [MATH: \textrm{GCF}(4a,8b) = {\color{red}{4}},] so:
[MATH: 4a − 8b|=; (4 ⋅ a) − (4 ⋅ 2b)]
2. Place the common factor in front of the parentheses, leaving whatever remains inside the parentheses:
[MATH: (4 ⋅ a) − (4 ⋅ 2b)|=; 4(a − 2b)]

---

Item 2 — Example: Factoring Out a Positive Number

Example Prompt:
Factor the following expression: [MATH: 6a+30.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We factor in two steps:

1. Separate the greatest common factor from each of the terms. In this case, [MATH: \textrm{GCF}(6a,30) = 6,] so:
[MATH: 6a + 30|=; (6 ⋅ a) + (6 ⋅ 5)]
2. Place the common factor in front of the parentheses, leaving whatever remains inside the parentheses:
[MATH: (6 ⋅ a) + (6 ⋅ 5)|=; 6(a + 5)]

Thus, the factored form of the expression is [MATH: 6(a+5).]

Item 6 — Tutorial: Factoring Out a Negative Sign

Content:
When the terms of an expression are negative, we can also factor out a negative sign. For example, the expression [MATH: -x-1] can be factored into [MATH: -(x+1).]

Content:
By the same token, the expression [MATH: -2x-2] can be factored by first factoring out a negative sign, and then factoring out the greatest common factor of [MATH: 2{:}]
[MATH: − 2x − 2|=; − (2x + 2)|=; − 2(x + 1)]

---

Item 7 — Example: Factoring Out a Negative Number

Example Prompt:
Factor the following expression: [MATH: -5a-35.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Both terms are negative, so we begin by factoring out a negative sign:

[MATH: − 5a − 35|=; − (5a + 35)]

Then, we continue factoring in two steps:

1. Separate the greatest common factor from each of the terms. In this case, [MATH: \textrm{GCF}(5a,35) = 5,] so
[MATH: − (5a + 35)|=; − (5 ⋅ a + 5 ⋅ 7)]
2. Place the common factor in front of the parentheses, leaving whatever remains inside the parentheses:
[MATH: − (5 ⋅ a + 5 ⋅ 7)|=; − 5(a + 7)]

Thus, the factored form of the expression is [MATH: -5(a+7).]
